title: Build a Personal AI That Schedules Your Life
description: A hands-on workshop. Build a Telegram bot that reads, creates, updates, and deletes your Google Calendar events — all from a simple chat.

children.text: Led by **Luca T.**

items: Build a Telegram bot that reads, creates, updates, and deletes your Google Calendar events from chat
Wire an AI Agent with a structured system prompt, dynamic date injection, and per-chat memory
Connect five scoped calendar tools using parameter descriptions as prompt engineering
Implement a security gate that stops unauthorized users at the canvas level — not in the LLM
Apply the four production-ready patterns that show up in every serious AI agent build
children.title: What you'll build

children.text: **What to have ready before we start**
Get these four things ready before the build. None take more than a few minutes — but you need them all before you can test anything.

items: An n8n account (cloud or self-hosted) — the workflow uses the AI Agent node and Data Tables
A Telegram account — to create your bot and chat with it
An OpenAI, Anthropic, or other LLM API key — powers the agent's reasoning
A Google account — the calendar you want the bot to manage

sections.title: 1. Prepare Your Credentials
sections.subtitle: Create your Telegram bot, get an LLM API key, and configure Google Calendar access

children.text: **What you're building — and how it fits together**

A Telegram bot wired to Google Calendar through an AI Agent in n8n. The agent reads your messages, decides which calendar tool to call, and sends back a formatted reply.

The full flow: Telegram → security gate → AI Agent (with calendar tools, memory, and contacts) → Telegram reply. Two parallel branches give you instant feedback while the agent thinks.

children.code:
Telegram message
             |
             v
      Telegram Trigger
             |
             v
   +------------------+
   | IF: chatID match |   <- security gate
   +------------------+
             | true
      +------+-------+
      v              v
Send chat action   AI Agent ---- Memory (per chat.id)
      |            |   |
      v            |   +-- OpenAI / Anthropic model
"Working on it!"   |   +-- Get events
                   |   +-- Create event
                   |   +-- Update event
                   |   +-- Delete event
                   |   +-- Get Contacts (data table)
                   v
            Send text message
            (MarkdownV2 escaped)
                   |
                   v
               Telegram

children.text: **Why n8n — and not the Claude app or Hermes?**

The Claude app can read your calendar, but you have to open it and ask. This bot lives in Telegram and responds the moment you text it — any time of day, without you touching a computer. That requires a deployment target, not an interactive session.

Hermes can build a similar bot faster, but it abstracts the pieces. This build wires everything by hand so you understand the architecture, not just the output.

The pattern is also model-agnostic. Swap OpenAI for Anthropic, Gemini, or a local Ollama model and the workflow doesn't change. Want Slack or WhatsApp instead of Telegram? Only the trigger and output nodes change — the agent core stays identical.

If you just want personal calendar management, the Claude app might already be enough. We're building this the long way because the architecture — trigger, security gate, agent, tools, output layer — transfers to every agent you build after this one.
Install Telegram and create a bot

items: **Install Telegram** if you don't have it: [App Store (iPhone)](https://apps.apple.com/app/telegram-messenger/id686449807), [Google Play (Android)](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.telegram.messenger), [Mac App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/telegram/id747648890), [Windows](https://desktop.telegram.org/), or [web.telegram.org](https://web.telegram.org) (no install).
**Find BotFather.** Open Telegram, search for `@BotFather` and confirm it has a blue checkmark. Tap **Start**. BotFather is the official Telegram account that creates bots.
**Create your bot.** Type `/newbot` and send it. BotFather will ask for a display name (anything), then a username that must end in `bot` — e.g. `my_scheduler_bot`.
**Save your bot token.** Once accepted, BotFather sends a token like `1234567890:ABCdefGHIjklMNOpqrs...`. Copy it somewhere safe — treat it as a password. Anyone with this token can control your bot.

**Start a chat with your bot.** Search for your bot's username in Telegram, open the chat, tap **Start**, then send any message (e.g. `hello`). The bot won't reply — that's expected. You're creating a chat record.

**Find your chat ID.** In a browser, open `https://api.telegram.org/bot<YOUR_TOKEN>/getUpdates` — replace `<YOUR_TOKEN>` with your token. You'll see JSON — find `"from": { "id": 987654321 }`. That number is your chat ID. Save it next to your token. _Troubleshooting: if you see an empty result array, send your bot another message and refresh._

children.text: Get an LLM API key

items: For n8n Cloud trials, OpenAI works out of the box with free credits. Any provider with an n8n Chat Model node works: Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, Mistral, or a local Ollama model.

1. Go to platform.openai.com
2. Create an API key under **API keys**
3. If you burn through the trial credits, set up billing

children.title: Anthropic

1. Go to [console.anthropic.com](https://console.anthropic.com)
2. Click **API Keys** in the left sidebar
3. Click **Create Key**

children.title: Gemini — recommended if you have org restrictions on API keys

children.text:
1. Go to [aistudio.google.com](https://aistudio.google.com)
2. Click **Get API key** in the left sidebar
3. Click **Create API key** in the upper right
Set up Google Calendar OAuth (self-hosted n8n only — cloud users skip this)

items: In n8n, go to **Credentials** in the left sidebar → **New** → search "Google Calendar OAuth2 API". Copy the **Redirect URL** n8n shows you.

In [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate), create a project, enable the Google Calendar API, create OAuth 2.0 credentials (select **Web application**). Paste the n8n Redirect URL into the **Authorized redirect URIs** field.
Copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret** back into n8n → click **Sign in with Google** → grant access.
Save the credential as `Google Calendar account`.

children.text:
Before anything else, you need an n8n instance to build in. The fastest path for a workshop is the cloud trial.

1. Go to [n8n.io](https://n8n.io)
2. Click **Get started** (or Try for free)
3. Pick a workspace name and a region
4. You're in. The trial gives you 14 days of full access to n8n Cloud — no credit card required.

The trial includes everything in this workshop: the AI Agent node, Data Tables, all integration nodes, executions, and credentials.

_After the trial, n8n Cloud has paid plans, or you can self-host n8n with Docker on your own server. The workflow JSON you build today imports cleanly into either, so the choice is reversible._

sections.title: 2. Create the Contacts Data Table
sections.subtitle: Build a controlled list of people the agent is allowed to invite — so it never invents an email address

children.text: **Why a data table and not Google Contacts?**

It gives you total control. The agent can only invite people you've added on purpose — no surprises, trivial to reset between runs.

In production you'd swap this for a CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce), a project tool (Linear, Asana), or Notion. The agent loop never changes. Only the tool you wire up changes.
In your n8n project, go to the **Overview** tab in the left sidebar, then click **Data Tables**
Click **Create Data Table**, name it `contacts`
Add two columns: `name` (string) and `email` (string)
Add 3–5 rows with real people you actually want to invite from chat
Keep the data table open — you'll need its ID when wiring up the tool in Step 6

Anything that already has the people in it:

- **CRM (HubSpot, Pipedrive, Salesforce):** invite clients you already track
- **Project tools (ClickUp, Asana, Linear, Jira):** invite task assignees automatically
- **Notion or Airtable database:** if your team's address book lives there
- **Google Contacts:** if you want the full personal address book and accept the risk

The agent loop never changes. Only the tool you wire up changes.
children.title: What you'd use in real production

sections.title: 3. Build the Entry Layer
sections.subtitle: Set up the Telegram trigger and the security gate that stops unauthorized users cold

children.text: **Security at the canvas level — why it matters**

Prompts can be jailbroken with creative phrasing. A node-level filter cannot. Security belongs in the canvas, not in the LLM.

If the IF node returns false, the workflow stops cold — no tools run, no tokens are spent, no calendar is touched.

Production upgrade: for multi-user deployments, replace the hardcoded chat ID with a lookup against a Postgres table or a data table of authorized users.
Create the Telegram Trigger

items: Create a new workflow (click **+** → **Workflow**)
On the canvas, click **Add first step** → search **Telegram Trigger** → select triggers "on message"
Credentials: click **Set up credential** → **Access Token** → paste your bot token from Setup
Trigger On: select `message`

children.text: Add the security gate (IF node)

items: Click **+** after the trigger → search **IF**
Left value / Value 1: `{{ $json.message.from.id }}`
Operator: **Number** → **Is Equal to**
Right value / Value 2: your chat ID from Setup
Turn **Convert types where required** on
Connect the trigger's output to this IF node

children.title: The workflow fires but nothing happens

children.text: Check the IF node — the `from.id` comparison fails silently if your chat ID is off by one digit. Copy-paste the ID instead of typing it.

sections.title: 4. Build the Instant Feedback Layer
sections.subtitle: A typing indicator and confirmation message — on a parallel branch so they add zero latency to the agent's answer

children.text: **Why parallel and not in front of the agent?**

AI agents take 3–15 seconds to reply. In a chat UI, that silence reads as 'is this thing broken?'.

These two nodes run on a separate branch out of the IF node. They fire at the same moment the agent starts — not before it. Zero added latency to the answer.
Add the typing indicator

items: Add a **Telegram** node → **Action in an app** → search **Telegram**
Configure the node with:
- **Credential:** Telegram account (from Setup)
- **Resource:** Message
- **Operation:** Send Chat Action
- **Chat ID:** `{{ $json.message.chat.id }}`
- **Action:** Typing
Connect from the **true** output of the IF node

children.text: Add the confirmation message

items: Add another **Telegram** node after the typing indicator
Action: **Send a Text Message**
Chat ID: `={{ $('Telegram Trigger').item.json.message.chat.id }}`
Text: `Working on it!`
Additional Fields → Append n8n Attribution: **off** | Parse Mode: **HTML**

children.text: The typing indicator is the native Telegram UX cue, but it's subtle. The 'Working on it!' line confirms in plain text that the bot received the request and is thinking.
children.title: Why two signals?

sections.title: 5. Build the AI Agent
sections.subtitle: One node — but the configuration matters more than any other step in this workflow

children.text: Add the AI Agent node

items: Click **+** in the upper right → add the **AI Agent** node
Connect the **true** output of the IF node to it
Source for Prompt (User Message): **Define Below**
Prompt (User Message): `{{ $json.message.text }}`

children.text: Write the system message

items: Inside the AI Agent node, click **Add Option** → **System Message**
Structure it in clear sections: Role + Context block, then a section for each tool
For each tool: cover when to call it (with example phrases), when NOT to call it, and how to call it (parameter format and edge cases)
End with an Output format block and a Constraints block (never invent meetings, never invent emails, never delete without confirmation)

children.label: System message: Role + Context block
children.prompt:
Role
You are a personal calendar assistant that helps the user check
and reason about their schedule via Telegram. You have access
to their Google Calendar through tools.

Current context
Today is: {{ $now.setZone('Europe/Rome').format('cccc, yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm') }} (Europe/Rome).
Always interpret relative dates ("today", "tomorrow", "monday",
"this week") relative to today.
children.prompt_note: Replace the timezone string with your own (e.g. 'America/New_York'). The $now expression resolves at runtime on every single message — the LLM has no real concept of today without it.

children.text: Connect the language model

items: Under AI Agent → Chat Model → add **OpenAI Chat Model** (or your provider)
Credentials: your API key from Setup
Model: start cheap — `gpt-4.1-mini`, `gpt-4o-mini`, or equivalent

children.text: Connect memory

items: Under AI Agent → Memory → **Simple Memory**
Session ID: **Define below**
Key: `={{ $('Telegram Trigger').item.json.message.chat.id }}`
Context window: leave at default (5)

children.text: The LLM has no real concept of 'today'. Without `{{ $now }}` in the context, 'tomorrow' becomes a hallucination roulette. The expression resolves at runtime, every single message.
children.title: Why inject the date dynamically?

children.text: The work this agent does is parsing dates, picking the right tool, and writing two-line replies. Start cheap, measure quality on real conversations, upgrade only if you see real failures. A bigger model rarely fixes a vague prompt. A tighter prompt almost always fixes a small model.
children.title: Why a small model?

children.text: Each chat keeps its own isolated context. No cross-contamination between users, no leaked schedules.
children.title: Why key memory to chat.id?

children.text: Simple Memory lives in n8n's process and vanishes on restart. For production, swap it for a Postgres-backed memory store.
children.title: Simple Memory doesn't survive restarts

sections.title: 6. Connect the Calendar Tools
sections.subtitle: Wire four Google Calendar nodes as tools — the agent decides when and how to call each one based on the parameter descriptions you write

children.text: **Parameter descriptions are prompt engineering**

The agent reads the `$fromAI` description to decide how to fill each field. Vague descriptions equal malformed dates and surprise behavior. Treat these strings like part of your system prompt — they are.
Get Many Events

items: Under AI Agent → add a **Google Calendar Tool** node
Resource: **Event** | Operation: **Get Many**
Calendar: pick your calendar from the list
Turn on **Return All** → click the sparkle button to let AI determine

children.text: Create Event

items: Add another **Google Calendar Tool** | Operation: **Create**
Calendar: select your preferred calendar
Start: enable AI definition (sparkle button), then paste the Start description below
End: same — sparkle button, then paste the End description below
Additional Fields: enable `summary`, `description`, `attendees` — sparkle button for each. Examples: Summary: `Event Title` | Description: `Optional event description or notes`
Also add **Conference Data** → select your video provider for auto-Meet links

children.label: Start parameter description
children.prompt: Event start datetime in ISO8601 format, {INSERT YOUR} timezone. The current year is 2026.

children.label: End parameter description
children.prompt: Event end datetime in ISO8601 format, {INSERT YOUR} timezone. The current year is 2026.

children.text: Update Event

items: Add a 3rd **Google Calendar Tool** | Operation: **Update**
Event ID: AI-defined. Description: `The ID of the event to update. Retrieve it first with the Get tool if not already known.`
For each field (start, end, summary, description): sparkle button + description

children.label: Start / End parameter description for Update
children.prompt: New start datetime. Only set if the user asked to change the time.
children.prompt_note: Without the 'only set if asked' wording, the agent will sometimes pass every field on every update, silently overwriting things the user didn't ask to change.

children.text: Delete Event

items: Add a 4th **Google Calendar Tool** | Operation: **Delete**
Event ID: AI-defined. Description:

children.label: Delete Event ID description
children.prompt:
The ID of the event to delete. Only call this tool after the user
has explicitly confirmed the deletion.
children.prompt_note: This single sentence is what makes the bot ask 'are you sure?' before deleting. Without it, a casual 'remove my Monday meeting' would delete immediately.

children.text: While configuring the AI Agent, n8n's built-in chat interface lets you test your system message and model behavior in real time before you wire up the calendar tools. This is much faster than running the full workflow repeatedly. Try a few test prompts to verify the agent understands your intent.
children.title: Use n8n's AI chat to test your system message

sections.title: 7. Connect the Contacts Tool
sections.subtitle: Give the agent a controlled list of people it's allowed to invite — so it never invents an email address

children.text: Add a **Data Table Tool** node from the AI Agent's Tool connector

items: Tool Description: **Set Manually**
Description: `Get list of contacts and use the names to select the email to invite to events.`
Operation: **Get** | Data Table: select your `contacts` table | Return All: **on**

children.text: Add a contacts rule to your system message inside the AI Agent node

children.label: System message: Contacts tool rule
children.prompt:
Tool: Get_Contacts
Call it BEFORE creating an event whenever the user mentions
people by name. Match names case-insensitive. If a name is not
found in the table, ask the user for the email. Never invent
email addresses.
children.prompt_note: Hallucinated email invites are the kind of bug clients remember forever. The rule is explicit, the data source is controlled, and the fallback is a clarifying question — not a guess.

children.title: The agent invents email addresses

children.text: Either the system prompt doesn't instruct it to call Get_Contacts first, or the data table tool isn't connected to the agent. Check both.

sections.title: 8. Build the Output Layer
sections.subtitle: The agent produces a text reply, but Telegram in MarkdownV2 mode is strict about special characters

children.text: Add a Telegram node after the AI Agent

items: Operation: **Send Message**
Chat ID: `={{ $('Telegram Trigger').item.json.message.chat.id }}`
Additional Fields → Append Attribution: **off** | Parse Mode: **MarkdownV2**

children.text: Paste the MarkdownV2 escape expression into the Text field

children.label: Text expression
children.prompt_note: Telegram's MarkdownV2 mode requires escaping a long list of reserved characters. Without this regex, the agent will eventually output a date like 15/05/2026 or a sentence ending in a period, and Telegram will silently reject the whole message.

children.title: Messages are missing characters or formatting is broken

children.text: You forgot the MarkdownV2 escape regex, or you switched parse mode without updating it. Either fix the regex or switch parse mode to plain text.

sections.title: 9. Test It
sections.subtitle: Activate the workflow and run the smoke test sequence to verify each part of the system

children.text: Toggle the workflow to **Active/Published** in the top right — the Telegram Trigger only fires when active
Send these messages to your bot in order

head: Message
What to verify
rows: Friendly reply, no calendar tool fired (check execution log)
Tool fired with today's date window, sensible summary
Reuses memory if possible, otherwise fetches
`add a call with <real contact name> tomorrow at 10`
Get_Contacts fires first, then Create with the right email
`add a call with Nonexistent Person tomorrow at 10`
Asks for the email — doesn't invent one

children.text: For each run, open the execution view and check

items: The AI Agent's input (your message + system prompt + memory context)
Which tools the agent decided to call — and which it skipped
The tool outputs
The final reply

children.text: If something's wrong, open n8n's AI builder chat (the chat icon in the editor) and tell it what's happening. It can run through your entire flow, spot missing connections, catch logic errors, and even suggest fixes. It's like having a debugger that understands your workflow.
children.title: Use n8n's AI builder chat to debug your entire workflow

children.text: Spend 10 minutes scrolling through five executions and you'll understand the system prompt's effect better than any documentation.
children.title: The executions view is where you learn how the agent thinks
The bot doesn't reply to anything

children.text: Check that the workflow is active — the Telegram Trigger only fires when active. Also verify the IF node: the `from.id` comparison fails silently if your chat ID is off by one digit.

children.title: The agent calls the calendar tool for 'hi'

children.text: Your 'When NOT to call' rules in the system prompt are too weak. Add explicit example phrases. The model needs concrete examples, not abstract categories.

children.title: Dates resolve to the wrong year

children.text: Pin the year explicitly in the `start` and `end` parameter descriptions, and inject `{{ $now }}` at the top of the system prompt. Both layers matter.

children.title: 'Working on it!' arrives after the agent's reply

children.text: Network jitter — Telegram doesn't guarantee message order across separate API calls. If it bothers you, drop the confirmation message and keep just the typing action.

items: A secure entry layer that filters by chat ID at the canvas level
A parallel feedback layer for instant UX — zero latency added to the agent's answer
An AI Agent with a structured system prompt, dynamic date injection, and per-chat memory
Five tools wired through `$fromAI` with carefully written parameter descriptions
A controlled contacts source that prevents hallucinated email invites
An output layer that handles Telegram's MarkdownV2 escape rules
children.title: What you built today

children.text:
**Four production-ready patterns in every build**

You also learned the patterns that show up in every serious AI agent:

1. **Security at the canvas level** — not only in the prompt
2. **Feedback in parallel** — never in series with the slow path
3. **Memory keyed by a real session boundary** — never global
4. **Tool descriptions as prompt engineering** — not as docstrings

That's the foundation. Everything else is variation.

children.title: Production checklist

children.text:
- Replace Simple Memory with Postgres-backed memory so context survives restarts
- Replace the hardcoded chat ID with a lookup against a user table
- Add error handling on tool nodes
- Set a model fallback if your primary model is down
- Log conversations to a database for quality review
- Rate-limit per user to prevent runaway costs
- Lock down credentials with proper OAuth scopes (read-only where possible)
- Document the system prompt in version control so changes are reviewable
- Test the MarkdownV2 escape with unusual characters in event titles

children.title: Where to go next

children.text:
**Quick wins on this workflow**

- **Add voice input.** Telegram sends voice notes. Add an OpenAI Whisper transcription step before the agent.
- **Add proactive reminders.** A scheduled trigger that runs every morning and pushes a daily briefing.
- **Add a second calendar.** Extend the system prompt with a 'which calendar?' rule, then add a parallel set of tools.
- **Replace Telegram.** Swap the trigger and output nodes for Slack or WhatsApp. The agent core stays the same.

**This is a pattern**

What you built is a calendar agent. What you actually built is a pattern: a chat entrypoint, a security gate, an AI Agent with a structured system prompt and memory, a set of tools, an output layer. The only thing that changes is the toolbox.

Every agent follows the same shape: entrypoint → security gate → structured prompt → model → memory → tools → output. Once you internalize this, every new agent is the same workflow with different parts swapped in.
